content.text: I've spent years building and tuning my personal systems to help me be happier, healthier, more productive, more intentional, and more giving! It all started back in college when I read
and wrote my first personal mission statement. Since then, I’ve gone through 20+ iterations – honing in on a system molded to how my brain works!
Some parts are second nature, some are experimental, and some more are future expansions!
below as well. I hope you find some of this useful and definitely hit me up if you have any thoughts, feedback, or suggestions!
“Systems engineering is the attempt to keep at all times the larger goals in mind and to translate local actions into global results.”
who I am, what I believe, and the cues to make it automatic.
Where I want life and career to go and the current bets to move towards it.
Reviews at different timescales that keep daily action and long-term direction aligned.
The routines that translate direction into allocations, projects, tasks, and calendar time.
Ways to catch blind spots, seek outside judgment, and turn useful feedback into changed behavior.
Systems for parts of a full life so productivity does not crowd out relationships, health, money, home, inner life, or fun.
The software and agents that implement the system.

Note: if you add up all the planning here you get ~6% of total time spent doing deliberate planning / strategy. I expect emergent planning through unanticipated opportunities to bring the real total closer to 10%. This is in line with what studies show is optimal for the explore exploit tradeoff!

A running list of tools I’m testing as possible replacements or additions to the core stack.
What I've seen work with my friends is starting as small as possible. A 10-second Daily Scorecard gives you a streak + real evidence and the one-sentence note gets you in the habit of reflecting.
is where I'd go next for Weekly planning + a personal mission.
is my favorite map for choosing small, controllable techniques that change behavior.
Take 10 seconds at the end of every day; after a few weeks, you have real data to ask why some days go better than others.
: ≤10 words on what most shaped the day
Once you have seven daily rows, spend 20 minutes reviewing the pattern + choosing the next week.
: Put the first steps on the calendar
Use a recurring pattern from the Daily + Weekly to choose one Weekly Tweak.
: Test for one or two weeks / measure / adopt, iterate, repeat, or drop

Most of this system is a synthesis of ideas I stole from people much smarter than me! The books below shaped the systems above most directly. (more here:
The bible and original inspiration for my personal mission statement, principles, roles, and Weekly planning!
My favorite bridge between personal strategy and the actual allocation of time across work, relationships, and purpose.
A wide-ranging look at the conditions behind a good life, especially relationships, purpose, virtue, and the gap between conscious plans and the rest of the mind.
: Helped me reconcile grit with strategic quitting, exploration, relationships, and designing around my own intensifiers.
Gave me the cues-and-environment mechanics behind my smallest repeatable behaviors.
A broad, evidence-based menu of ways to change beliefs, emotions, habits, relationships, and decisions.
The playbook behind my project-based approach to learning through direct practice, focused drills, and fast feedback.
The reason I protect long blocks of focused time and treat the calendar as part of the system.
My starting point for feedback loops, delays, leverage points, and the ways a local fix can hurt the full system.
A practical framework for making decisions under uncertainty and separating decision quality from outcome luck.
The source of my obsession with optionality, bounded downside, and systems that get stronger through stress and experimentation.
Made the case for explicit decision rules and outside feedback by showing how predictable our biases are.
My favorite structured framework for comparing career paths by impact, fit, career capital, and option value.
A practical argument for protecting the vital few by giving the rest a real no.
Made me take broad exploration and cross-disciplinary experience seriously as long-term advantages.
The best counterweight to over-optimization: choose deliberately, accept tradeoffs, and experience your life while it is happening.
The book that pushed me to think about saturating Dunbar's number through repeated time, vulnerability, trust, and dependable support.
: The practical source for building relationships through generosity, consistent follow-up, vulnerability, and connecting people before I need anything.
The framework I use for high-stakes conversations where emotion and disagreement can shut down dialogue.
Taught me to separate appreciation, coaching, and evaluation so I can use feedback even when it arrives badly.
